newsitem.title: USA: Wall St seen opening with election victory party.
newsitem.headline: Wall St seen opening with election victory party.

text.p: U.S. stocks should open sharply higher on Wednesday as Wall Street cheers the re-election of President Bill Clinton and Republicans winning the battle for control of Congress.
"We'll see a big hurrah at the opening," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
The long bond rose sharply in early trading after an overseas rally, knocking its yield to a fresh low of 6.57 percent, the lowest since March 7.
Standard & Poor's December futures jumped 3 to 718.4 before the opening of trading, indicating a positive opening.

"Both Clinton and the Republicans keeping Congress is very positive for the stock market and the bond market and that Mr. Yeltsin survived his operation is also another big plus for global economies," Cardillo said.
Overnight, world markets rallied. The Tokyo Nikkei surged 399 points to end just below 21,000 and Hong Kong stocks stormed into record territory. In London, the FTSE 100 rose 6.5 to 3927.
"But as we move close to new highs, I would expect a levelling off as the future of the economy comes into play. We could see some bumpy days ahead," Cardillo said.

Drug and biotechnology stocks stand to benefit from the election, he said, since a Republican Congress would not give the President much room to change the U.S. healthcare system. Technology stocks and financial stocks could also gain.
No major economic news is due today. The second leg of the U.S. Treasury's three-part quarterly refunding auctions begins later. The government is due to offer about $10.0 billion in 10-year notes.

U.S. shares in London moved higher, spurred by news of the outcome of the Congressional races. Investors had by-and-large discounted the Clinton victory, but worried about whether the Republicans, seen as more fiscally conservative, would be able to maintain their majority in Congress.
The dollar rose in Asia but was off earlier highs in Europe.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column says Deutsche Telekom AG's mega-billion dollar IPO has not stirred much U.S. interest.

The New York Times Marketplace column reports that the Nastional Association of Securities Dealers is trying to change arbitration rules in terms of the timings of arbitration as well as punitive damages.
